newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan rejects China's conditions for talks.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan rejects China's conditions for talks.

text.p: Taiwan on Monday refused to drop its drive for international recognition, scorning China's pre-conditions for ending an 18-month-old freeze in Taipei-Beijing talks as unreasonable and impossible.
Hong Kong's Wen Wei Po newspaper quoted China's top Taiwan negotiator as setting four conditions for reopening a dialogue across the Taiwan strait that Beijing halted in June 1995.

The pro-Beijing daily quoted Tang Shubei as demanding that Taiwan stop its drive to join the United Nations, stop sending its leaders to countries that recognise Beijing, stop dual recognition and stop importing large amounts of advanced arms.
Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council issued a flat refusal.
"Communist China's demands are unreasonable. There is no way we will agree to such conditions," vice chairman Shi Hwei-you was quoted by the official Central News Agency as saying.
"The conditions are simply impossible," Shi said.

The exchange of political salvoes came as Taiwan foreign minister John Chang was returning from a trip to South Africa, where he failed to persuade Pretoria to reverse a recent decision to sever ties with Taipei and recognise Beijing.
The loss of South Africa would leave Taiwan with only 29 diplomatic allies, mostly small, underdeveloped states in Africa, central America and the Pacific.

Shi's cabinet-level council is Nationalist-ruled Taiwan's top body for making policy towards its communist arch rival, which has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province ineligible for foreign ties since a civil war split them in 1949.
"Taiwan is a member of the international community. It should have parallel contacts with other countries," Shi was quoted as saying.
She said the island's "pragmatic diplomacy" policy of wooing international friends was unrelated to Taipei-Beijing talks.
Council chairman Chang King-yuh said the government would follow the "people's will" in developing its China policies.
Chang, speaking on state-run television, said the door for negotiations with China was always open and that Taipei would would wait patiently for the resumption of talks.
A furious Beijing suspended talks with Taiwan indefinitely after President Lee Teng-hui succeeded in making a landmark private visit to the United States in mid-1995.
China said the visit showed Lee wanted Taiwan's independence despite its avowed advocacy of reunification with the mainland.
Drawing a dramatic line against independence, China rattled Taiwan with war games and missile tests in nearby waters in the run-up to the island's March 23 presidential election.
Beijing won China's U.N. seat from Taipei in 1971 and seeks to block Taiwan's efforts to join international forums.
Another council vice chairman, Kao Koong-lian, blamed Beijing's hostility for the cross-straits deadlock.
"Communist China should not impose its own thinking on us..." Kao told reporters. "This kind of attitude is the major barrier blocking the development of ties across the strait."
